newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Prince Charles sails to the Philippines.
newsitem.headline: Prince Charles sails to the Philippines.

text.p: Britain's Prince Charles on Thursday sailed into Manila Bay in heavy rain, arriving from Hong Kong where he attended ceremonies to hand over the territory to China.
Prince Charles, who on Monday surrendered Hong Kong to China after 156 years of British rule, planned to spend just 10 hours in the Philippines before flying back to London.
But, as with the day of the handover in Hong Kong, rain poured down on his arrival in the Philippine capital, forcing some of his programme to be cancelled.

After briefly stopping to chat with officials and British school children, the Prince was driven off to meet President Fidel Ramos who had promised to make it a happy visit after the emotional ceremonies in Hong Kong.
"If you watched the (handover) ceremonies, there were a lot of tears," Ramos told reporters, adding the heir to the British throne would be treated as a head of state.
"We try to make it as joyous and happy as befits any reception that we have given to heads of state and heads of government coming to this country," he said.

Manila was under British rule for a few months in 1762 when its troops overpowered the Spanish colonial government there. It was returned the following year to Spain which ruled until the end of the 19th century.
Guests of the luxury Manila Hotel by the shore gathered on their balconies as the Britannia -- which Ramos called the "most classy royal yacht" -- steamed into the bay.
The visit affirmed that Britain's commitment to Asia did not end with the handover of Hong Kong, British ambassador Adrian Thorpe said.
"(It) sends a clear signal that Britain's partnership with Asia will continue as strongly as ever," he said.
It may also help Britain's efforts to be a key supplier as the Philippines military goes on a shopping spree to replace an ageing navy and add to its handful of fighter planes.

The yacht, also carrying Britain's last governor in Hong Kong Chris Patten and his family, was accompanied on its journey by three patrol craft based in Hong Kong until the handover and sold to the Philippine Navy.
During the brief visit, the environment-conscious British heir will be presented with two endangered Philippine tarsiers, the world's smallest primate, which he will immediately give back.
The large-eared and saucer-eyed tarsiers have been flown to Manila from their home in the south of the country where they have been tamed for the occasion.
After the give-and-give-back ceremony, the primates will be formally declared an especially protected species and flown back to their island home.
